speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, October 20, consideration of the motion of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett Prime Minister) for approval of the trade agreement entered into at Ottawa the 20th day of August, 1932, between representatives of His Majesty's government in Canada, and His Majesty's government^ in the United Kingdom, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the fiscal changes consequent thereon.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in this debate may I say I am fully conscious of my great responsibility, and the duty to my constituents who did me the honour to send me here
as their representative. Further, I am not unconscious of my responsibility as a Canadian citizen and a British subject. In common with every hon. member on this side of the house,
I had an open mind in regard to the results, whatever they may have been, coming from the Imperial economic conference. I made up my mind that if out of the conference came results which, after due trial, worked towards alleviating the dire distress in this country, they should have the sympathetic support of hon. members on this side of the house. But Mr. Speaker, after carefully studying the articles and the agreements I am free to admit that of all the great blunders that this government have made since they came into power in 1930 this is perhaps the greatest blunder of all. I am not going into the by-election in South Huron-unless my hon. friends across the floor draw me out-except to say that I marvelled that the government brought on the by-election in South Huron four days before the opening of parliament. I had a suspicion that there was method in their madness, that they had something to conceal. Now I am sure of it. Knowing South Huron as I do, I want to tell the Prime .^Minister and the government that if they had waited, had called parliament and tabled the results of the imperial conference before holding the by-election, the majority in South Huron instead of being 2,000 would have been 4,000.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to be as fair as I can to the government. I want to give them all the credit I can-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
-for God knows that if ever a government needed some credit it is this government. So I want to be as sympathetic as I can with the government. To my mind the results of this conference should be regarded in this way: are we satisfied that the results as we know them will give wider markets to the basic industry of this country, namely agriculture, at increased prices? Will it give wider markets at increased prices for the other basic industries, the products of the mines, of the forests, and of the fisheries; and is the consumer and the vast army of unemployed with their wives and families, getting a fair, square, honest deal through the agreements that have been brought down in this house? On the other hand we must consider, and consider carefully, whether the manufacturers' association are getting more than they are entitled to. Are they getting concessions in high protection that will enable them to plunder, if you like, the consumer, the

farmer, the unemployed and people who are struggling for existence in this country. If we review the whole situation in that light 1 am free to confess, much as I would like to support the government-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

They

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
No, I know they are doubting Thomases. I am free to say that, reviewing it in that way, there is nothing in it to give any consolation to the people of Canada.
Now, if the house will have patience with me, I want to go back to the war. I do not want to say anything more than this, that the economic conditions that prevail not only in this country but in every country in the world can be traced back first to the war, with its great loss of life and great destruction of property, and the huge debts that it entailed; also to the mad rush for money, the greed for money, not only on the part of individuals but corporations and countries. There is another factor, that of higher and higher tariffs. I believe that the imposition of higher tariffs-and this country is as guilty as any, especially under this administration -has perhaps done more to stifle trade and commerce and bring us into the condition in which we find ourselves today than anything else.	'
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) speaking in this house, the sevens teenth in this debate, elaborated for some minutes what he called the sheltered market that the government of which he is a member has obtained for exports from this country under this treaty. He said it was a sheltered market. Well, a sheltered market means a protected market. When I say that I do not refer to tariffs. Sheltered means shielded from storm and stress and strain, a place of safety. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce thinks sending our wheat to Great Britain under the provisions of this treaty at world prices is sending it into a sheltered market, then he has a different opinion of a sheltered market from mine. The same applies to flour, and to many other commodities. If there is any market which is not a sheltered market to any degree it is that fierce competition of buyers and sellers on world markets. The United Kingdom will take our wheat at world prices. In my humble opinion the preference of six cents a bushel is hardly worth the paper it is written on, it will not enhance the price of wheat shipped to Great

Britain one iota, and when the Minister of Trade and Commerce talks about sheltered markets I think he has something else in mind, the sheltered markets the manufacturers are going to have is the Dominion of Canada under this treaty-if I have time I will come to that in a moment or two. But in regard to wheat and flour I want to point out to the house that, having considered it as earnestly and as conscientiously as I can, I have come to certain conclusions. I have inquired carefully from men whose business it is to export Canadian wheat to all the markets of the world, and from men whose business it is to make flour in Canada and export it if they can, and the information I have received is this, that the preference of six cents a bushel on wheat will not avail anybody anything, and the ten cents a barrel protection on Canadian flour will not help the Canadian millers.
The same may be said of article 5, which deals with cattle. I will not take time to read it; I will say that if through this treaty anything is done to increase the exports of cattle from this country to Great Britain will be a help, but under present conditions, with the rate of exchange as it is, I do not think this means anything. I know of a large shipment of prime cattle that left western Ontario about a month ago. They were sold in Great Britain, and the net result of the sale was 4 cents per pound after all charges were paid. Is that a sheltered market? The shippers lost thousands of dollars on those cattle, and if nothing better comes out of this agreement it will not amount to anything.
Now for a moment or two I should like to deal with bacon and ham, and if the house will bear with me I should like to read article 6, which covers these products.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: The hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor) dealt with that question.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I may deal with the
hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Gott) if he does not keep quiet. Article 6 reads as follows:
His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom declare that it is their intention to arrange as soon as possible after receiving the report of the commission now sitting on the reorganization of the pig industry in the United Kingdom, for the quantitative regulation of the supplies of bacon and hams coming on to the United Kingdom market and undertake that in any legislation which they may submit to parliament for regulating the supplies of bacon

United Kingdom
and hams from all sources into the United Kingdom, provision will be made for free entry of Canadian bacon and hams of good quality up to a maximum of 2,500,000 hundredweight per annum.
Is there a single commitment in that article, Mr. Speaker, which obligates His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom to increase the purchase of Canadian bacon and ham? This provision is surrounded by ifs and whens and hows, and in any event nothing can be done until the report of this commission is brought in. I want to make this prediction, that if in course of time the export of Canadian bacon and ham should reach the figure mentioned in article 6, the farmers all over this dominion will go into hog raising on a large scale, and instead of increasing the price of hogs the price will decrease. The price is $3.75 now, and it may go even lower. There is another feature entering into the matter as well. The farmer will have nothing to say with regard to the price received for bacon in the English market. The huge packing monopoly of this country will control the price; they will not only increase their business but will milk the farmers who raise the hogs which they buy. So if this article is viewed reasonably and carefully the conclusion must be reached that there is nothing in it for the farmers.
Now I want to come to another important article, that dealing with eggs, poultry, butter, cheese and other milk products. I will not read article I, but at the end of that article I find these words:
... set forth in schedule A appended hereto.
Schedule A appears on page 53 of the supplementary report of the conference, and reads as follows:
As regards eggs, poultry, butter, cheese and other milk products, free entry for Canadian produce will be continued for three years certain. ^ His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom, however, reserve to themselves the right, after the expiration of the three years, if they consider it necessary in the interests of the United Kingdom producer to do so, to review the basis of preference so far as relates to the articles above enumerated and, after notifying His Majesty's government in Canada either to impose a preferential duty on Canadian produce whilst maintaining preferential margins, or in consultation with the Canadian government to bring such produce within any system which may be put into operation for the quantitative regulation of supplies from all sources in the United Kingdom market.

My purpose, therefore, in speaking today is to deal with matters emanating from the more or less relevant topics which have so far been discussed in this debate.
One of the most perplexing questions taxing the intelligence of the Canadian people today is that of state participation in industry, or the degree to which control should or should not be exercised therein. For many years this problem has been of paramount interest, but at no time has a final solution been more to be desired than in this unprecedented post-war period of financial stringency and economic chaos. My purpose is not to enter into any metaphysical or philosophical discussion of the causes of control, but rather to draw attention to the extreme necessity of an intelligent policy that will prevent a virile people from wallowing in degradation, from disintegrating in idleness, and from starving to death in the midst of plenty, because governments the world over in their vacillating impotence are unable to

For, Mr. Speaker, in my mind civilization is not a standard, but a continuous creative process requiring two simultaneous impulses, the cooperation that consists of the fulfilment of a common desire, and that which comprises the pooling of

United Kingdom
separate, individual contributions. It is a matter of bringing capital and labour into closer harmony and cooperation with one another, or the destruction of capitalism and the super-imposition of a new system in its place.
The future must decide whether the worker is to be the cause or effect of his work; whether he is to control the means of production in the interest of himself and the many, or be controlled through them in the interest of the few. Herein lies a question, that of competency. Labour has often been charged with too much heart and too little brains, just as capital is said to suffer from too much brains and too little heart; but who in this house will say, in view of the serious condition in Canada today, that the capitalist has either heart or brains? I have always felt that the world is subject to change, that all we know has been derived from the experience of the past and the experimentation of the present. The processes of evolution, according to Lincoln Steffens, show that nothing is ever done finally or right, and that nothing is ever known absolutely or positively. The trouble with human beings is that they become too sure of themselves, that they become too much attached to old fashioned ideas in new fashioned times. We will take for example the lovable member for Weyburn; we know he believes that the abolition of tariff is a cure for all evils. Yet, even an expert as able as the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore) is confident that a little tariff tinkering will get us out of the present world difficulties and that a little patching of the system will help a great deal. Here is what he has to say:
We used to hear a lot about tariff tinkering. The tinkerer is a useful man in the community.
The hon. member for Ontario believes in patching, but may I remind the house that there is a limit to which the old garment can be patched. If the world crisis is to be solved by tariff tinkering, all the changes in the customs tariff made while the opposition were in power would, in the language of the Ottawa Citizen, have as much effect upon the situation as a small garden hose would have on a large forest fire, or the waves on the rise or fall of the tides. The trouble with most of us is that unwittingly we are slaves to old ideas and the unwilling disciples of new ones.
The small group in this corner of the house suggest going off the gold standard, depreciating or inflating our currency. The hon. member for Weyburn protests in these words: "No, no; the monetary policy or reform cannot hold a candle to the tariff, so far as importance is concerned." And while he makes that statement one could not help but notice the simultaneous nod of approval, a sort of "absolutely Mr. Gallagher, positively Mr. Shean" attitude on the part of hon. members sitting behind him. The incantations of this Liberal tariff medicine man fills the sick Canadian patients with awe, but leaves their health absolutely unchanged. Likening our tariff to an appendix he would cut it out, in order that the patient may live happily ever afterwards. Suppose, however, the patient is suffering from a more serious, a vital disease, such as heart trouble. As one writer has described it, finance is the heart of our economic system, and when once its effectiveness becomes impaired hon. members know quite well what may happen. Credit is the life-blood of our commerce and industry, and when the heart stops furnishing the body with blood the body dies. In like manner when our monetary system goes bad the rest of the body politic is bound to suffer.
The present difficulty, Mr. Speaker, is essentially financial. In my view tariffs are but the means to protect the present gold standard. As has been pointed out by Sir William Beveridge, head of the London School of Economics, the first point to remember is that we are faced with a money crisis. There is a breakdown in the machinery of exchange and the regulation of production by prices. The outstanding feature of the present condition is a general fall in prices, measured in terms of money. It was Lincoln Steffens who asked Albert Einstein, scientist and philosopher, how he had been able to discover anything new. Mr. Steffens reports the answer and comments upon it as follows:
His answer is the answer. He did what he did by challenging an axiom. That's what our statesmen who can't find the way out of depression are unable to do. They cannot challenge an axiom. And that's what some of our boys and girls will have to do. They will have to challenge a lot of axioms, and my suggestion to all parents and teachers is to teach the children no axioms, nothing positive, but everything as the more or less tested theories and hypotheses of us old dubs, whose most valuable heritage for our children is a definitely taught body of conscious ignorance, obvious failure. Then maybe they will be free minded enough to see why we could not distribute plenty and leisure, make peace in the world, and remove the causes of war, graft, and incompetence.
That, Mr. Speaker, is exactly what the hon. member for Weyburn will not do. He will not challenge an axiom. In this connection I quote the words of John Stuart Mill:
A greater number of people cannot in any given state of civilization be collectively so well
618	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
provided as a smaller. The niggardliness of nature and not the injustice of society is the cause of the penalty attached to over-production.
T believe the changed conditions of today, the introduction of machinery and the applications of scientific methods have shown that such is no longer true. As pointed out by Henry George:
The very reverse of these propositions is true. I assert that in every state of civilization a greater number of people can be better provided for than a smaller. I assert that the injustice of society and not the niggardliness of nature is the cause of the want and misery which the current theory attributes to overpopulation.
Henry George's attitude, as the antithesis to that of Stuart Mill's, to me proves that nothing is known positively and completely. There is no doubt that orientation in regard to the functions of government has changed considerably during the past few decades. As far back as the close of the eighteenth century no less an economist than the great Adam Smith made this pronouncement:
Government does not have any other aim except that of increasing the wealth of its subjects.
But in the judgment of our twentieth century statesmen this condition can be brought about only by the ingenuity, selfreliance, adaptability and resourcefulness of individual effort. Generally speaking, I think this is so, but there are different kinds of individual effort. There is the commendable activity of the plebeian bread-winner who provides for his family on the one hand, and the rapacious manipulations of the unscrupulous patrician financier on the other. The struggle for emancipation from the rule of the latter class has continued down to the present day with varying success. Certain social changes and services have been achieved through the daily and persistent activities of reformers, while other aims unfortunately have been attained only by resort to violent revolution. It is said of the Bourbons that they never learned anything nor did they ever forget anything, and so ruling classes, unable to read the 'handwriting on the wall, the signs of the times, have been ruthlessly overthrown never to return.
But we have had many examples of this cycle repeating itself. Changed conditions I think demand new methods of approach. For what else are these revolutions of which I have spoken, Mr. Speaker, but struggles, as one writer put it, to batter down a system of life linked to means that no longer exist, and to trample underfoot the thousand obstacles which faith, morality and tradition have put

in the way of the industrial, economic, philosophic and scientific progress towards which all classes turn. We have in Canada to-day obstacles in wider variety and greater range than ever existed before. For the first time in our history this country is actually threatened-no doubt about it-with starvation in the midst of plenty. The present so-called "great age of industrial progress" has developed deep-rooted defects which jeopardize the very existence of capitalism unless they are remedied. Foremost among these defects I contend is the lack of proper balance between production and consumption, or the difficulty of distributing the vast mass of agricultural and manufactured products to a consuming public bereft of the means of purchasing the necessaries of life. In this corner of the house we believe the fundamental cause of the depression is attributable to the breakdown of finance, in other words, the failure of money to function as a medium of exchange and a measure of value. We believe that the machine age has introduced a whole series of new situations to which the old categories do do not apply, and that the next stage of development cannot possibly retain the old laissezfaire attitude. We believe that the solution of our fundamental economic problems must be worked out by preserving the best features of individual initiative, yet gaining the advantages^! collective effort, and that as a guiding principle the ideal of service must be accepted in lieu of the pursuit of economic reward. Hon. members will agree that science has given us a new world, But it has also left many tremendous difficulties in its wake. I think, however, the fault lies not in science as such, but rather in the wrong application of science. The simultaneous existence of wealth and poverty, the tragic march of progress resulting from the use of machinery, has forced people to check up on themselves, and so more and more are men the whole world over beginning to realize the necessity for a thorough-going reconsideration of old tenets, precepts and ideas, or as one writer put it, a revaluation of all ideas.
We live in an age of transition, we are imperceptibly passing into a new age. Meanwhile all these battles of ideas are going merrily on. The average citizen, I take it, is bewildered by it all, fearful lest the social fabric give way under the strain. The inr telleetual, pondering over the pages of history, notes the destruction of other civilizations in similar crises and deduces a similar fate for our own. But I believe that while there is life there is hope, a hope that is embodied in the spirit of exact knowledge inspired and infused

United Kingdom
with the scientific spirit, and utilized to avoid what I consider the world's great twin evils, reaction and revolution. Reaction and revolution, overproduction and underconsumption, passion, prejudice, unreason, these all can be solved by looking at things in terms of basic reality untrammeled by preconceived ideas or mutilation of facts.
I believe the world is suffering from a breakdown of finance, but nothing is done-I believe all governments have the same fault-except the policy of aimless and hopeless drift. In a country such as this American continent where, as one writer said, money has always been the aim of all social effort, the money lender, the banker, is allowed to reign supreme. The farmer, sitting behind his plough, may poetically be said to be monarch of all he surveys, but the products of the field, the very land on which he is living, are rapidly passing from his control to that of the king of the castle on St. James street. This is accomplished by a period of deflation, and the sheriff is allowed to do the rest. Thus poverty and misery have increased, the dollar becomes unstable, prices fluctuate, unemployment increases, and the purchasing power of the people is reduced to nil. Meantime the money lenders are grabbing off everything worth while, and will not resume business until all their bad debts are wiped out by the people, and governments have unloaded upon the taxpayers losses which should be borne not by the poor but by the financial sharks who, I claim, have created them by their policy of vicious deflation in their periodic drive to skim off the cream, thus sweeping more and more wealth into still fewer and fewer hands.
What a strange thing this bugbear of credit has become. How easy it was to get credit before 1928, and how hard it is to get it today. Only a very small handful of money is available now in comparison with that what was available before 1928. By holding to the gold standard, by forcing currency down, and by hoarding money, the financiers have time and again set their own price on the release of credit. You may call it money if you will, but it is not money; you could not take it away from them at the point of a shotgun. You cannot get it in any way except by their voluntary act and deed. The farmers in my district have not the credit they need. Credit is available only when you can put up those good notes and securities and pay the interest. I claim that the farmer in the west, who has been producing wheat for less than the cost of production during the last few years, cannot put up those good notes and securities which the banks demand. One writer has said that
Christ was betrayed for thirty pieces of silver. Today suffering humanity, as represented by the farmers of the west, is being betrayed for thirty pieces of gold. It is said that all the gold in the world could be put in a space thirty feet long, thirty feet wide and thirty feet high. There is no question but that the farmer is being crucified on a cross of gold.
The recent deflation of credit has hurt no one as much as it has hurt the farmer. The price of wheat now is so low that he cannot possibly meet the obligations which he incurred before the depression. What makes the situation so bad is that other commodities have not fallen in the same ratio, while freight, interest rates, taxes and the cost of public services for the most part actually have gone up. Therefore I believe the government would be well advised to relieve the situation by a general scaling down of the liabilities of the farmers. For the life of me I do not see how a farmer can be expected to continue indefinitely to produce for less than the cost of production, pay his taxes, send his children to school and meet all the other obligations which are imposed upon a citizen of Canada today. I say there is something radically wrong with a system that penalizes the basic industry of the country to the extent I have indicated. It seems to me, therefore, that the only alternative is a change to a system which will bring about a more equitable distribution of wealth as well as of goods and services generally. When one recognizes the fact that the aggregate tangible wealth of the Dominion of Canada amounts to about thirty billion dollars, apart from our natural resources, and that agriculture accounts not only for the greater portion of Canada's net wealth, but also for a portion of net income greater than that produced by any other industry, the knowledge gained therefrom should awaken us to the gravity of snowing under an industry from which ordinarily so many blessing should flow but which, like the goose that laid the golden egg, is being killed to the detriment not only of other industries but of all people in all walks of life.
I repeat that the financial policy of this country should be altered. The very fact that banks no longer are willing to extend the smallest amount of credit is an admission on their part, I believe, of the bankruptcy to which the system has driven the farmer. It may be all right to say that this crisis is the result of an act of God or a law of nature; nevertheless one cannot gainsay the fact that it is due to inherent defects in the system itself. I have supported resolutions presented in this house asking for a wheat
620	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
bonus. I think that while the farmer is producing for less than the cost of production he should have a bonus to tide him over the bad times from which he is suffering. Therefore I should like to put myself on record as being in favour of a bonus, not of five cents but of twenty-five cents if we can get it. When the five cent bonus legislation was put through this house some time ago one member asked another whether he was going to be insulted by the bonus, and whether he would take that five cent insult. The member replied, "Well, I would rather be insulted to the extent of twenty-five cents, but if I oannot get a twenty-five cent insult, I will take the five cent insult." I am willing to be insulted to the extent of twenty-five cents, but if I cannot get that I will accept very willingly the five cent insult.
Think of the ridiculous and yet tragic position in which the farmer finds himself to-day, trying with wheat at 25 cents to pay a mortgage incurred when wheat was selling at $2, and think of the far greater number of bushels the farmer must raise now to pay off old debts. Is it fair to compel the debtor farmer to pay in a medium so unreliable and so dishonest? In common justice there should be a scaling down of the indebtedness of the farmers.
I have a resolution which I should like to put on Hansard before my time is up. It reads as follows:
Honoured Sir,-
Are you aware that the Finance Act of Canada was conceived and made statutory when our country was facing a national crisis; and that in the year 1923, advantage was taken of the position secured by the chartered banks under the said act, to further consolidate their privileges, in such wise that they are now in position to absorb the sovereignty, as well as the rights and duties of the government and people of Canada?
Under the provisions of the act as it now exists, provincial and municipal governments can only obtain advances, on their bona fide securities, from chartered banks, at an interest of not less than five per cent per annum; whereas the banks themselves may obtain these advances from the government of the people of Canada at a present maximum of three per cent per annum. Thus is presented the ridiculous anomaly of the people borrowing from itself to enrich private corporations.
To remedy this evil we earnestly recommend the amending of the Finance Act, so that, upon the deposit of approved securities, the provinces and/or the municipalities may obtain advances direct from the government, instead of being compelled to use the medium of the chartered banks.
So far as I am concerned the Bank Act can be revised tomorrow, if that will mean something towards alleviating the distress of the farmer in the west; for I repeat that

something must be done to relieve the present unbearable situation in which he finds himself. The other day the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore) expressed it as his opinion that the ship of state should not sail to uncharted seas; he likened the nations of the world to ships which, in time of storm such as the present, should be safely moored to what he called a central buoy, represented by the gold standard. Experienced sailors have told me that in stormy weather it is far safer to put out to sea than to be moored to any central buoy; Mr. Moore, however, prefers to be more than ever moored to the gold standard.
We are told that the only way to bring the two major problems of production and consumption into their proper relationship is by reducing production and increasing consumption. In view of the fact that it now takes more goods to pay debts, reducing production would entail too many hardships, and it would also tend to increase unemployment, turning more people out of work. Increasing consumption can be brought about only by increasing purchasing power, and here is where the government should step in with a more vigorous and constructive policy. Why not put more money into circulation? Why not build the Peace River outlet, about which the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) has been talking so much in this house? Why not start something in connection with the St. Lawrence waterway? Inflation alone would not do much good without inaugurating such a building policy as I have suggested. The government can, at will, either directly or indirectly, increase the purchasing power of the Canadian people. It can increase it directly by continuing the wheat bonus, to which I have referred; it can do it by scaling down debts, it can do it by building the Peace River outlet; it can do it by inaugurating housing schemes such as have been advocated by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote); and it can do it by loaning money to certain utilities in this country which, by means of such loans, could put more people to work. It can do it indirectly by depreciating or inflating our currency.
We have all listened to the able speech delivered by the hon. member for Macleod in which reference has been made to the manner in which Australia is rounding the corner. We have been told how the depreciation of her currency has given her such a tremendous advantage in the world's markets, and how in comparison a premium on Canadian currency has seriously handicapped our producers. The hon. member for Macleod

United Kingdom
pointed out that the Australian grower, with his nine cents a bushel bonus, is getting over 80 cents while the Canadian farmer obtains only 26 cents. That is possible because the British pound is worth $3.85 in Canada while it brings over $6 in Australia. We w'ere further told of the scaling down of 22| per cent in interest rate on mortgages in Australia. Why can we not do something of that kind in Canada? Either let us improve on what we have in order to relieve the situation temporarily, or let us live a little more dangerously in order to live.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess

I wish to give an idea of the condition in which we in the province of British Columbia find ourselves. There are a few mills running, but production is very small. The product from those mills is not of a type which would help us to any great extent. Our natural resources are being dissipated and nobody is being helped. For instance, a report was published in the press that a large order had been placed by Great Britain for British Columbia lumber. A month or so ago, before I left that province, I went through the part of the country from which this order was being supplied, and I found that all they are getting is $8 per thousand alongside the ship, Vancouver harbour. Hon. members will realize there is very little profit in that. 1 am sorry to say most of the work on this particular order is being done at the mill by Hindus.
The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Fraser), could tell of the distress in his riding so far as the lumber business is concerned. A short time ago a mill situated at Giscome in the Cariboo district was sold. In the sale were included the mill building and boarding houses, in all about fifty or sixty buildings. There were 8,000.000 feet of lumber in the yard and 16,000,000 feet of logs in the lake. Although in better times this mill would have been valued at $1,500,000, the whole jack-pot sold for $85,000-mill, buildings and lumber, which in normal times would have been valued at about $3,000,000. Their trouble is they are situated inland and cannot handle offshore
business. The ten per cent preference would do them no good whatever because they depend entirely upon the markets available in the United States and the prairies, and particularly the United States. The mill was erected with the aid of American capital for the purpose of shipping to the United States. That is one instance, and I could give many others almost as bad.
At the annual meeting of the North Vancouver Board of Trade held a short time ago, the chairman, Captain Cates, a prominent business man in that section of British Columbia, made a speech. His remarks as reported in the press under date of October 21, are as follows:
It is true that Canada has received a preference on lumber in the British market, but it is doubtful if this will be of much assistance to our British Columbia lumber industry. Against this preference we are handicapped by the great distance between ourselves and that market as well as the proximity of European producers to Great Britain.
So stated Captain J. H. Cates, President of the Board of Trade, in his annual report to the board on Thursday night. Lower standard of living of European competitors which make possible lower cost of production, was also cited as a factor with which the lumber industry of this province has to contend.
"We who are in business in this city, depend largely on our lumber industry and the export of wood products," stated Captain Cates. "Our markets for these products have principally been United States, Japan and our middle west. At present these markets are practically barred to us."
Captain Cates explained that the United States impediment is the prohibitive tariff. In Japan continued depreciation of the yen is the big factor and in the middle west it is the low price of wheat which has greatly reduced the purchasing power of the prairie farmer. Captain Cates declared that until these conditions are remedied there is little hope for much improvement in the lumber industry.
The trouble with the lumber industry so far as the agreement is concerned lies in the five year term, or we might term it the five year plan. At the present time the consumers in the middle west and the United States are not worrying, because they are not buying lumber. They have been getting their lumber from the Pacific coast. The time will come, however, when they will want lumber in large quantities, and then they will wake up to the fact that the exorbitant prices they are paying are caused by the $4 duty on lumber from British Columbia. In my opinion there may be such an agitation in the United States against this duty of $4 a thousand that they will come to us and say: "What can you give us if we take this duty off?" We wni be in the position that

we will have nothing to offer. If we have to hang on by our shoestrings for another five years there will not even be the shoestrings left. In five years they will all be out of business. For that reason I am opposed to the treaty. We should be in a position to negotiate with the United States to have this duty, which amounts practically to an embargo, removed. When in Washington there was lobbying for the imposition of this duty on Canadian lumber, one of the arguments used was "Canada is getting a New Zealand preference, also a preference from Australia and the United Kingdom; yet they are getting our business." That is all right. I was in favour of the . New Zealand treaty, and I am in favour of enlarging our market in Great Britain as far as possible, but not at the expense of losing a market we have enjoyed ever since I can remember. Geographically the market in the United States is the logical one for Canadian wood products. Since I began business in the lumber industry we have shipped to the American market; that has been our big source of trading. Any lumberman in this house or anywhere in Canada will state that that is where he made his money-from lumber sold in the American market. The five year plan, however, puts us in a position, as I see it, whereby we cannot do any bargaining to have that duty removed.
The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) the other evening was very much concerned about the unemployed in the United States, who number, he said, eleven million people. Before leaving the coast I had the pleasure of listening to three or four addresses over the radio by Mr. Roosevelt, the democratic candidate for president of the United States. He was emphatic in stating that in his opinion the high tariffs were the cause of a great deal of the unemployment, and he pledged himself at every meeting that one of the first things he would undertake would be, the reduction of tariffs to a reasonable standard. The United States of course started this tariff war back in 1928, and I figure they are the prime offenders. But now they have an election on, and I think my good friend from Nanaimo will get his answer on the 9th of November as to whether the people of the United States think high tariffs are the proper thing.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill)made reference to the difference in transportation on lumber from Scandinavian and Russian ports to Great Britain as against shipments from the Pacific coast, and after

allowing for the 10 per cent preference there would still be a balance of $3 per thousand in favour of the Scandinavian and Russian shipments. I have figured this out and I find he was very conservative in his estimate.
The hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), who spent, he says, five months plus the time of the conference as lumber expert advising the government, no doubt has been a successful business man in his line and has shipped a good deal of lumber to the United States, but I think in this instance his judgment was biased. I do not suppose there was anyone in Canada more disappointed than he was when instead of getting twenty per cent they got only ten per cent. He said this about the committee's conclusions:
A tariff preference of twenty per cent will, we are confident, enable us to overcome high production costs, long distance from markets, etc., and compete against any country in the world with the exception of Russia. With regard to the latter country we cannot suggest any preference that would enable us to meet the class and character of the competition that Russian economic and marketing methods present.
I am not going to say anything about Russia. I believe that any industry should pay a fair wage. I do not think anyone should be allowed to dump any kind of product on any market at less than the fair value. But we have this situation facing us: in time Russia is bound to be a factor in the lumber situation. They have more timber in Russia than we have on this whole continent, and it is obvious that some day it is going to be marketed.
Then in reference to the five year plan, the hon. member for East Algoma said:
I come now to the five year period for which the agreements have been signed. Personally I look upon that length of time as one altogether too short. I have the consolation however, that no government coming into power in Canada will presume to make any attempt at interference with these agreements. As a matter of fact all governments will look upon them in exactly the same sense as the delegates looked upon them; all governments will consider the agreements as the beginning of a great scheme of inter-empire development. In regard to the stipulated time, I say without hesitation that many of the industries which will ultimately profit by the agreement cannot hope to reap full advantage from them within a space of less than five years.
If we have to wait for five years a lot of people depending on the lumber industry will go hungry in the meantime.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the leader of this government (Mr. Bennett).
I have a great admiration for him; I think he is a very clever man. He is a man of action, and he is boss on the job. I think any

United Kingdom
leader of a government should be the boss, and I wish I could say the same thing of the leader of the British Columbia government. But the Prime Minister also makes mistakes. I sympathize with him in his difficult task. Any leader of a government, handling the biggest business in the whole of Canada, is bound to have troubles in these strenuous times. But in my opinion he is not a good organizer. I was very much surprised when he selected his cabinet. He had an abundance of material to choose from, business men who have been tried and proved, but instead of building up his cabinet with first-class business men he turned to the professional class. I do not wish to Ibe personal, but it is generally conceded that professional men are as a rule not good business men. I think he has too many professional men and not enough good farmers or good business men-of course they may be good politicians. I would like to refer to one glaring example, that is, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryckman). If there is any department of this or any government we ever had in Canada that is as unpopular to-day as the Department of National Revenue, I do not know it. To-day you do not know what you are going to have to pay to-morrow by way of tariff, and that has been the condition for months and months. That is not business; it is not common sense.
Just one word in conclusion in reference to unemployment. The situation is very serious, and there does not seem to be the organization there should be. Speaking of our own province of British Columbia, when I went home in June I was interviewed by several delegations from municipalities. I rvent to Victoria with the representatives of two municipalities. The deputy finance minister of British Columbia said: We cannot buy your bonds; they are no good; we cannot lend you any money; your credit is no good. I said to him,-and I would like to be corrected if I am wrong,-"I understood the Prime Minister, Mr. Bennett, to say that nobody would 'be neglected; everyone would be taken care of. If the municipality could not borrow the money, if its credit was not good, the province was to borrow that money from the federal exchequer, lend it to the municipalities and take their promise to pay." But they knew nothing about it. So I say, sir, that there should be some definite plan, no matter what it is, to work on, if we are to avoid a lot of misunderstanding and a lot of suffering.
Speaking of loyalty to the empire, I am a Canadian, and I am just as loyal as any other Canadian. At the same time, while everything else being equal we prefer to trade within the empire, we believe that with our immense 53719-40
natural resources we must have also a world market.

Mr. Speaker, every hon. member of this house ie the keeper of his own conscience and is responsible, by voice and vote, only to his own constituents. But I must express my surprise and regret at the fact that the proposed legislation giving effect to the conclusions arrived at by the imperial conference has been received in the manner that has been indicated by hon. gentlemen opposite. In my innocence and simplicity I had thought this would have received some favourable consideration and that it would have been accepted at least as an instalment, a step in the direction of the extension of empire trade, but it seems that no good thing can come out of Nazareth. From beginning to end, with scarcely an exception, no word of approval of any portion of the agreement has been uttered from the other side of the house.
In all sincerity I say that I do not believe these gentlemen reflect the opinion of the great majority of the Canadian people. The Liberal party of this country attributes to itself the introduction of the first preferential tariff towards Great Britain, and that is true if you call lower duties upon imports a preferential tariff. I call it rather jughandled. I would not inflict upon the house reminiscences of more than forty years ago, when hon. gentlemen opposite stumped this country from end to end in favour of commercial union with the United States, but for a parallel of their sudden conversion to a new faith you must go back to the story of Paul on the road to Damascus, for in one night these gentlemen deserted the policy of commercial union or, as it was softened in terms, unrestricted reciprocity with the United States, and came out as the proponents of a preferential tariff towards Great Britain. Is this house aware, and do hon. gentlemen realize, that the policy of preferential trade with Great Britain as designed by the Liberal party of nearly forty years ago has been a signal, a dire and an utter failure? I make that statement advisedly, and I am going to give the house proof.
In 1896, the year before the preferential tariff was introduced, imports into Canada from the United Kingdom amounted to 31.2 per cent of our total imports. In 1930, thirty-four years after the preferential tariff was introduced, the percentage of our total imports which came from Great Britain had been reduced to 15.2 per cent, or cut literally in half. It came into office two years ago on a policy of protection, and it.does not propose to sacrifice the industries of Canada upon the altar of empire or any other country. Let that be well understood. However, apart from the protective features, apart from those interests which require the encouragement and shelter of a protective tariff, there is a large avenue of trade which can be cultivated to the advantage of the sister nations of the commonwealth. It is those avenues which are attempted to be exploited by the agreements reached in Ottawa.
There is one subject of prime importance which has been touched upon now and again, here and there, in this discussion, that of currency, credit and exchange. No more involved, no more intricate, and no more difficult subject is today before the minds of economists than that of currency, credit, and exchange. In my opinion not only is it worthy of the most serious consideration, but it may be that some step will have to be taken towards restoring a parity between the Canadian dollar and the pound sterling if means to that end can be found. But 1 would point out this, that the exchange situation has absolutely no relation to and no bearing upon the resolution now before this house; none whatsoever. Whether the house accepts or rejects the resolution now before us it will have no bearing whatsoever upon the money end of the question. I am well aware of the difficulties that the wheat growers of the west and other producers in Canada are having because of the low price of the pound sterling in comparison with the Canadian dollar, but you cannot improve that condition by accepting or rejecting this resolution. This resolution has no more to do with that than have the Greek kalends. Let us deal with that subject in due course when we reach it. Because there was failure at the recent conference to devise any plan of a monetary character is no reason for refusing to accept what is before us.
Many other arguments have been put forward-for instance, that the hands of parliament are being tied. I do not think anybody takes that argument seriously. The hands of the British parliament are also being tied, but nobody is protesting against that-yes, a few are protesting; the gentlemen who left the nationalist government in Great Britain

do Object, but they are an exceedingly small minority.
Again it is said that the duration of five years is too long. It has been pointed out that the late government made a treaty binding Canada for twelve years. Personally I would be rather disposed to complain that the term is not longer than five years, believing as I seriously do that the results of these pacts will be of great advantage to Canada.
Our friends on the other side are very solicitous about the extension of the trade of Canada to foreign markets. The hon. member who last spoke talked about the United States market for the lumber industry. Suppose we admit all that, for the sake of argument, at any rate. Where do we get? Nowhere. Every country in the world has raised its tariff against every other. Since the abrogation of the Elgin-Marcy treaty with the United States in 1865, a long time ago, the United States has never been willing to enter into any commercial treaty with Canada that was worth a hoot, and I say that the prospects will not be altered very much in the present state of affairs under either Mr. Roosevelt or Mr. Hoover. But the cry is for foreign markets. Never mind this pact for better markets within the empire: it is foreign markets that hon. gentlemen want.
Those steady patriots of the world alone.
The friends of every country but their own.
Let me conclude with a story perhaps familiar to you all, one that was current many years ago when we were fighting the battle against the then policy of commercial union with the United States. It runs like this: An English pedestrian walking along a highway in Ireland met Paddy driving a little pig ahead of him on a string. The Englishman stopped him and he said: "That is a nice little porker you have there." "Yes sir," said Paddy. "Where are you taking him?" "I am taking him to market," said Paddy. "How much would you get for a little porker like that?" asked the Englishman. "It may be a matter of three or four shillings." "Oh," said the Englishman, "why, if you had that pig in London you would get four pounds for him." "Yes," said Paddy, "and if I had the Lakes of Killarney in hell I'd get a shilling a glass."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter now before the house has been under discussion for almost two weeks, and one might naturally conclude that almost every argument that could be put forward either pro or con had been worn almost threadbare. I have noticed as I sat here listening to the debate the arguments

United Kingdom
advanced by those who sit to your right. There has been nothing but enthusiasm for this agreement on the part of those 138 good men and true, who all see eye to eye in connection with this trade agreement. I have noticed that those who sit to your immediate left, Mr. Speaker, some ninety in number, take just the opposite view. They are unable to see anything good or worth while in this trade agreement. They are able to show certain features in connection with it which are not commendable, and strange to relate, all of them, some ninety in number, seem to see eye to eye. It strikes me as strange when so many good intelligent men on one side take one view, without any division among them, and so many good intelligent men on the opposite side view the matter in an entirely different light and can see no good whatever in it.
In this corner of the chamber, though small in numbers, there is an honest division of opinion among us. Some of us see in the trade agreement certain points which commend themselves to us, while on the other hand some of us see in the same agreement certain items which do not commend themselves. The previous speaker gave a most instructive address based on trade matters affecting both the United States and the United Kingdom for a period of years past. I hold the personal view, and I do not fear to express it, that the United States is our best customer -if she would let us trade with her. That great country immediately to -the south of us, stretching the full length of our southern border from east to west, holding within its confines a population of about 120,000,000 people, with its large urban -centres, offers to us markets for the products of our primary industries which cannot be excelled. In that country we see a market for the products of our farms, our forests, our mines and the seas. There would seem to be a ready market in those thickly settled centres to the south of us. I purpose to deal at this time with trade conditions as they have existed between Canada and the United States for the past ten or twelve years.
I have before me The Commercial Intelligence Journal of October 22, 1932, in which I find a comparison between trade figures for the month of September 1920 and the same month of 1932. No doubt hon. members will find these figures most interesting. Although a number of commodities are mentioned, I have selected only four; as I am chiefly interested in farming, those commodities deal particularly with the farm. In the month of September, 1920, Canada exported to the
United States market 1,478,469 bushels of wheat on which there was no duty charged. In September, 1932, last month, at a time when there was a duty of 42 cents a bushel against our wheat, we exported only twenty bushels. In that commodity alone the figures show there has been a drop from almost a million and a half bushels down to twenty, and in that time the duty has been raised from free to 42 cents per bushel.
Then, dealing with cattle, we find that in the month of September, 1920, we exported 37,569 head on which no duty was charged; in September, 1932, we exported 666 head. In the meantime the duty has risen to a point where on cattle up to 700 pounds in weight the rate was 21 cents a pound, and on cattle over that weight, 3 cents a pound. Of course the increase in duty caused the decrease in the number exported. Let us examine the figures as they apply to butter. In September, 1920. there was a duty of 2i cents a pound against our butter, and under that duty we exported 4,500 hundredweight. In September, 1932, we exported only 23 hundredweight, because in the meantime the duty had risen from 21 to 14 cents per pound. In September, 1920. we exported 23,676 dozen eggs on which no duty was charged. Last month we exported no eggs at all to the the United States. In the meantime the duty had risen to ten cents a dozen.
There are 43 items on this list, and with regard to each a similar story could be told. In 1920, twenty-five of those items were on the free list, and the remainder were subjected to only a very low tariff. If we check the statistics for the month of September, 1920, we find that the exports to the United States were very considerable. But when we look at the figures for the month of September, 1932, we learn that each of those 43 items has had a high tariff rate registered against it. and the exports are very low indeed.
During that twelve year period from 1920 to 1932 what has been the attitude of the United States towards Canada? As I have stated, in 1920 most of the commodities were free of duty. In September, 1922, the Ford-ney-McCumber tariff bill became effective. Through that legislation wheat was removed from the free list, and began carrying a duty of 42 cents a bushel. Cattle were raised from the free list to 1^ and 2 cents a pound, butter was raised from 2i to 12 cents a pound, and eggs from free to 8 cents per dozen. In the month of June, 1930-and I ask hon. members to take particular notice of the month-the Hawley-Smoot tariff bill was passed by the United States government. By that legislation the duty on wheat remained at 42 cents per

Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
bushel, but the rate on cattle was raised to 2J cents and 3 cents per pound; the duty on butter was raised to 14 cents per pound, and on eggs to 10 cents per dozen. I do not intend to go into details as to the other items; I have given the figures only as evidence of the attitude of the United States towards us. By two successive steps between the year 1920 and the present time they raised the duties on a large list of commodities which materially affected the quantity of trade between that country and Canada.
What has been the Canadian attitude during that period? When in 1922 the United States tariff on our wheat was raised to 42 cents per bushel, our tariff on American wheat was only 12 cents per bushel. When in the same year the United States tariff on our butter was raised to 12 cents per pound, our tariff on American butter was only 4 cents. When they raised their tariff to 14 cents we were very patient and long-suffering, choosing to leave ours at 4 cents. Probably by our lack of retaliation we showed a commendable attitude. A most interesting factor in connection with this trade review is that in the twelve months ending March, 1930, according to trade statistics, Canada imported from the United States 1,146,205 bushels of wheat and exported 6,804,099 bushels. When we come to the twelve months ending March, 1931, Canada imported a little over 148,000 bushels and exported over 10,000,000 bushels. Now, that is rather a strange situation. I might perhaps emphasize here that our duties on wheat were raised in the month of September, 1930, to 42 cents a bushel. Yet we exported more than we did the previous year when the duty was lower. The same applies to butter. In the twelve months ending March, 1930, when the tariff on butter was four cents a pound, we imported over 176,000 pounds and exported over 20,000 pounds. For the next twelve months, ending March, 1931, we imported a little over 26,000 pounds and exported over 70,000 pounds. That struck me as very strange. I figured it out in percentages, and I find that by raising the Canadian tariff against American wheat we decreased our imports from the United States eighty-seven per cent and increased our exports over thirty-four per cent; we decreased the imports of butter over eighty-five per cent and increased our exports seventy per cent. Another point in connection with that is that the increased tariffs were not in effect for the full year but only from September, 1930, to the end of March, 1931, some six and a half months. If any hon. gentleman cares to trace that a little further and take the next year's imports and exports he will find that in comparison

with 1930 it shows the same favourable situation.
Now, after looking at the United States tariffs, and our tariffs towards them, I would like to ask the question: Is the attitude of the United States towards us changing in any respect? A couple of years ago some one thousand university teachers, professors and economists visited the White House, urging the president to review the tariffs of the United States, because they were having an adverse effect upon American trade. Rather a strange feature is this, that on October 17, 1932, just ten days ago, the Journal of Commerce, published in New York, carried the headlines:
180 Economists Ask President Hoover to Lower Prohibitive Tariffs.
Hold that Rates Defy Sound Economics, Strangle Trade, Spread Unemployment.
The article continues:
Attributing to the rates of duty in the Hawley-Smoot tariff law the strangling of commerce and the spread of unemployment, members of the faculties of various educational institutions throughout the United States today called upon President Hoover to use his official powers to remove the world trade barriers occasioned by this law.
They stated that the Fordney-McCumber Act of 1922 and the Smoot-Hawley law of 1930 caused foreign nations to retaliate.
Well, I would wonder if they did not, although it did take Canada a long time to retaliate. We were patient and long-suffering from 1920 through 1922, up through June, until September, 1930; then Canada did retaliate. The article goes on:
So that foreign trade in export value in 1929 amounted to $5,240,995,000, in 1931 $2,377,981,000.
A decrease of over fifty-four per cent. They further pointed out that for the first eight months of 1932 their exports were further reduced $500,000,000 below the same period of 1931.
I again ask the question; Is the attitude of the United States toward the trade she once enjoyed with Canada changing? My own opinion is that it is changing considerably, and that is one good feature that I see in connection with this trade agreement. It looks to me as though it is a club being swung over the heads of the people of the United States. It -may not be a charitable course to pursue toward a friendly and neighbouring nation, but let us bear in mind that in 1922 we received from the American law makers a very severe slap on one cheek, nationally speaking. In a docile manner we turned the other cheek and received a very severe slap on it in June, 1930. We were seripturally correct-

United Kingdom
"whosoever shall smite thee on the right cheek, turn to him the other also." That, nationally speaking, is what we have done. But, Mr. Speaker, I am reminded of a story I heard of a very orthodox preacher who taught what the Man of Galilee said in that respect. He ran across an obstreperous individual who endeavoured to try him out on it, and after some argument on a trivial matter his would-be persecutor hit him on one cheek. The preacher said: "Well, the Scripture says, whosoever shall smite thee on the right cheek, turn to him the other also'"; so he turned the other; and the man struck him on the other cheek. "Now'," the preacher said, "The scripture does not say what you are to do," so he waded in and gave the man a sound thrashing. Nationally speaking we received a swat on one cheek in 1922; we turned the other and received another good one in June, 1930.	1
think at that point we were scripturally correct in starting in to give the United States a good thrashing. In September, 1930, tariffs were raised against the United States, on the principle, as I think it was stated at the time, of "brick for brick." Now, while I advocate low tariffs and am a proponent of free trade, certainly if one nation puts its tariff against our wheat at 42 cents a bushel I cannot see any reason for keeping ours at 12 cents. Our tariff at that time was raised to a parity with that of the United States. This Canada-United Kingdom trade agreement is following along somewhat the same lines, that is, it is continuing to give the United States just a little bit of a thrashing, economically speaking. That is one good reason why I feel like supporting this trade agreement.
Another favourable feature I see in connection with the trade agreement is that it is diverting trade to our own mother country. While the United States is the natural country for us to trade with, if they refuse to do business with us I think the reasonable course for us to pursue, is to trade with the mother country. A large number of us here either came from the mother country or are descended from ancestors who did, and naturally our feelings turn in that direction.
Another feature I see in connection with this pact is that it lowers duties on many commodities that will be exchanged between Great Britain and Canada. It does not go so far as I would like to see it go, but it goes a short distance at least. While perhaps a number of steps were taken in the wrong direction, you might say, by increasing tariffs, this is a short step in the right direction by reducing tariffs on a number of commodities which we require and which we expect to secure from the mother country:
Another very important reason why I favour this trade agreement is that under it we have a preferred market in Great Britain for our Canadian wheat. Someone may ask whether we expect the price of wheat to be raised. Possibly it will not, but the United Kingdom offers to us the best market in the world for our wheat. There is no other country on the face of the globe that has been using, or is likely to use, as much of our wheat as does the United Kingdom. I can understand hon. members to your immediate left, Mr. Speaker, taking the stand they have taken. Possibly they are looking into the future, but members in this corner of the house would put themselves in rather a strange position, I think, if they took the attitude that they did not want a preferred market for Canadian wheat. I have before me a clipping from the Ottawa Citizen which points out that after November 15 the Irish Free State will be in an unpreferred position in regard to tariffs because the country failed to conclude an agreement with the United Kingdom at the Ottawa conference. As a result the Irish Free State will come under the ten per cent extra tariff after the middle of next month. If we reject this trade agreement, we say in effect that we do not want it. If the government did not have a majority sufficient to carry this agreement and we saw it defeated in this bouse, we would be in the same position as the Irish Free State; we would be subject to the extra 10 per cent on commodities passing between Canada and the United Kingdom and, in addition, we would have the extra charge of six cents per bushel against our wheat. I wonder how many farmer members of this house could go back to the prairies and justify a vote against a trade agreement which would have that effect. I represent a constituency that is entirely agricultural; my people grow wheat almost entirely, and I would hesitate to go back there and attempt to justify a vote against this agreement even though it does not give us all we might like. In the matter of wheat it does give us concessions that no one can deny.
Under this agreement we also get a free market for a quarter of a billion pounds of bacon and ham annually. That is quite a concession. It opens up to the Canadian farmer, both east and west, a market for pork products that in the future will be of considerable benefit to Canadian agriculture. It also gives us an improved live stock market, which will be of benefit to both western and eastern Canada. Our natural market for live stock in western Canada was the United States; they went by way of Winnipeg or
632	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
Calgary down to such large centres as Chicago, Minneapolis, Duluth, Denver and so on, but we cannot send them there now because there is a prohibitive tariff against them. Our only other market is Great Britain. It is true that this market is a. long distance away, but it is true also that the agreement makes available to us certain advantages in the live cattle trade that will be of at least some benefit to agriculture.
In addition, the fact that the recent Imperial economic conference was carried through to a successful conclusion has made it possible to call together the world economic conference which is to convene in the near future. We hope that this coming conference will be perhaps even more successful than the conference in Ottawa, especially in dealing with monetary questions, with the exchange situation and other problems.
I have given just seven reasons, Mr. Speaker, why I feel like supporting this trade agreement. I think they are quite sufficient. I can see in the agreement enough to convince us, as an agriculturist and as one representing a constituency interested in farming, that my constituency will be best served by having this agreement completed.
Mr. CHARLES E. FERLAND (Joliette) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, the constituency of Joliette which I have the honour to represent in the house, is semi-rural and semi-urban. Its adherence to the Liberal cause, almost traditional, clearly indicates its political preference. The people of this county have had the opportunity, in many elections, to show their opposition to England's military imperialism. In 1911, ignoring the advantages of the reciprocity treaty agreed upon, between Canada and the United States, under the leadership of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the greatest diplomat and most accomplished statesman that the French race in America has produced, they gave a slight majority to the nationalist candidate, notary J. P. A. Guilbault, notwithstanding the great popularity enjoyed by the defeated Liberal candidate, Mr. Adelard Du beau, since then appointed judge, in order to follow the policy of the great nationalist leader, the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), who was then at the height of his fame and was rightly considered, together with the standard bearers of the Devoir, as one of the foremost champions of the rights of the French Canadian minority of this country. Since that date, the people of Joliette have always sent Liberal members to the House of Commons, and in 1917, they unanimously manifested, together with almost all the electors of Quebec, their opposition to military
	.
imperialism as advocated by the Conservative party, whose present leader, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) proclaimed, in 1929, in the house, that when England is at war, Canada is at war.
The people of this dominion will be called upon at the next election to give their verdict on a new form of imperialism; economic imperialism, and on the high tariff policy of the Conservative party.
Since the election of 1930, a disquieting, enervating atmosphere, and a material and moral depression has spread over the land, and is felt in the county of Joliette as elsewhere, among the farming class as well as among trades people. The agreements entered into at the last Imperial economic conference in August last at Ottawa, rest essentially on an economic policy of imperialism and complete isolation. May I, sir, state that in my humble opinion, we should strongly and courageously oppose this new doctrine ol economic imperialism. From my viewpoint the main reasons which should guide us in our opposition to this new aspect of the Conservative policy, in Canada as well as in England, are the following: These imperial agreements, the right hon. Prime Minister admits it himself, are founded on Conservative principles, namely, the policy of very high protective tariff.
These agreements will result in forcing the rest of the world to pay Caesars tribute to the British Empire.
By erecting a tariff wall around the empire, isolating it from the other nations, these agreements will inevitably result in further restricting Canadian exports and greatly spreading unemployment.
The said agreements bind Canada for years, this will hinder the government from negotiating advantageous trade treaties with foreign countries, considering that economic conditions are ever changing in the world and Canada must therefore always be ready to modify and readjust its tariff to suit the occasion.
The imperial economic agreements are totally in contradiction with the recommendations and resolutions of the League of Nations to which Canada is a party. May I, by the way, take the opportunity of welcoming home, and in the house, Canada's representative at last year's League of Nations meeting: I refer to the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre), "my pair" in the political order of things, who played me the mischievous trick-I do not blame him-of preventing me from casting my vote during

United Kingdom
the whole of last session, because I had agreed, without knowing that he was sailing for Europe, to pair with him.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
These imperial agreements, founded on rejected principles by the League of Nations which advocates the lowering of tariff walls among all nations, are also disapproved by the world's greatest economists, because of the policy of imperialism and high tariff involved. The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) who just preceded me in this debate, stated a moment ago, that well known economists in the United States, and professors of the leading universities of that country-and he could have added of the world's most prominent economists-advocate at present lowering the tariff walls which are of a nature to disturb the peace of the world and increase disorder and all ills from which we suffer.
Might not these empire agreements result in provoking on the part of other countries where unrest prevails, retaliatory tariffs, which might be disastrous to Canadian trade and even to that of the other nations of the commonwealth?
The imperial agreements, which we are requested to approve, are also entirely contrary to the century old traditions of England's policy, and m our own country, to the principles which have regulated our interimperial trade since 1897, and conferred on Canada advantages the loss of which cannot be retrieved in the state of isolation of the commonwealth, even were London to become the financial centre of the universe.
Finally, the few particular advantages which might result from these empire agreements- there might be certain advantages, though I cannot discover any which would benefit Canada, as a -whole-these particular advantages, I say would not compensate Canada for the loss she would sustain in the rest of the world.
And, to conclude, the following is the last reason for my opposition:	The economic
structure of Canada, rests on a world foundation, closely bound to her international trade. The Conservative party, by its high tariff policy, has sapped the source of our vitality by restricting its field of action, to one world empire, even though the largest.
The main objections, from my viewpoint, which should prompt us to reject the agreements under consideration by the house, are these: Does not our political history teach us that Canada is an essentially exporting country and it cannot carry on its political and economic existence without an extensive exportation? I think we all agree on this point, Liberals, Conservatives, United Farmers, Independents, all proclaim the necessity of Canada exporting large quantities of products abroad, because our young country with its immense natural resources and small population cannot consume its entire production. Without a considerable foreign trade, without markets abroad to absorb our surplus production, we are bound to have a crisis and distress in this country. The causes of a crisis are numerous. What are the signs? The most apparent ones are first a drop in our foreign trade and unemployment. Unemployment is a direct result of the disruption in our foreign exports. What, however, is the main cause of this drop in our exports, if not the error made here, as in the United States and in all countries where the same distress prevails as in Canada, that policy, based on high protection, of the Conservative party?
The tariff policy of the Conservative party is essentially bad and ruinous for Canada, and the fact of its being applied to England or other parts of the British Empire does not improve it.
We judge of the value of a policy by its results.
Our country has known years of prosperity under the Liberal regime, from 1921 to 1930. Did not Canada, thanks to a foreign policy proportionate to her requirements, thanks to a large trade with all the countries of the world, attain, under Liberal rule, the fifth place among the trading nations of the world. However, sir, in less than two years, with the drop of our exports due to the high tariff of our Conservative friends, our country is now in the seventh place.
An hon. MEMBER (Translation): Shame!
