Is there,
sir, in Canada, any province, any county, any individual who would not rejoice, today, if it were possible, to bring back, by some miracle, the prosperity which we enjoyed from 1921 to 1930?
If our foreign and world trade is the key to our prosperity, we must note that, during the last years of the Liberal regime, Canada carried on a most profitable business with the entire world. Is it not known that, under the Liberal administration, we had invaded almost everywhere foreign markets, in the east as well as the west? Is it not known that, during the last years of Liberal rule, we traded profitably with all continents and that in every case the trade balance was greatly in our favour? If we figure out the
634	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
total of our foreign exports to Europe, Asia, Africa, Oceania and South America, we find that we sold to these continents more goods than foreign or Canadian ships brought back to Canada, and thereby, through a favourable trade balance enriched Canada and Canadians. Only the United States exported to Canada, during that period, more goods than they imported. I think that if we add to the apparent trade balance, all that remains invisible, namely that which does not appear in the statistics, such as United States capital invested in Canadian industries, and the money left in this country by United States tourists, about $300,000,000 per year, it will become evident that even in our trade transactions with the United States, under the Liberal rule, the trade balance was still greatly in our favour.
This government now endeavours to prove that the depression prevailing in this country is not due to its poor policy but to the fact that the crisis is world-wide, and, as remedy, it offers us the Imperial agreements which are under consideration.
I have shown, sir, that our trade relations must be international. Our trade relations with the British Commonwealth are not international, but constitutional in character. It is by virtue of our constitution, the British North America Act, of 1867, and of certain Imperial statutes, as interpreted in a number of Imperial Conferences, notably those of 1923 and 1926, and clearly defined by the recent Westminster statute, that Canada has become an autonomous nation in the British Empire, united to England and the other sister nations solely by a moral tie and by a common allegiance to our sovereign, the king.
Canada's bond of union with England and the other parts of the British Empire is therefore constitutional and not international in character. Just as Canada cannot carry on its economic existence independently of world trade or as the Dominions of Australia and New Zealand must resort to foreign markets to sell the surplus of their products or as England herself was obliged-to ensure her prosperity and power-to invade all world markets, or as any nation in the commonwealth cannot remain isolated, thus the association itself of all these sister nations is unable to exist, maintain or bring back prosperity to its people, independently of international or world trade. The principle of economic imperialism which is at the basis of the empire agreements, under consideration, had already been submitted to England, previous to the conference of 1923, by the leader of the Conservative party, Mr. Baldwin. How-
I Mr. Ferland.]
ever, this proposal which was rejected by the Imperial Conference of 1923, provoked in England an outburst of protests, not only among the opponents of the party in power, among manufacturers and business men, but in the very ranks of the Conservative party. And, shortly after, at the election of December, 1923 this economic policy was rejected by the people.
The well known French Economist, Andre Siegfried, who took part in the inquiries of the "Musee Social" in France, in cooperation with the Franco-British Association, and who is a distinguished writer, having published many books dealing with economic conditions in England, France, Canada, Germany and the United States, a person we can look upon as an entirely disinterested observer, tells us what were the feelings and views, in England, as a result of this policy introduced by the Conservative leader, at the Imperial Conference of 1923. The following is what he wrote in his volume entitled "England of Today," page 116:
The idea of a closed empire is in contradiction with the whole contemporaneous British tradition, which places in the complete liberty of trade the very foundation of national prosperity and has penetrated the British mind to a depth unsuspected by us. Some industrial centres may be under the spell of the preferential remedy. But exporters and business men as a whole cannot lose sight of the fact that England carries on two-thirds of its external trade with foreign countries, one-third of which form part of Europe. They must aver that in spite of the preference, British exports to the colonies have during this crisis fallen off in the same ratio as those destined to Europe. Accordingly they feel rather chary over engaging on a large scale in an experiment the purport of which is to replace foreign retail markets by those of the empire, for even though suoh a shunting and disconnection of trade channels were found to be feasible, it would take to say the least a whole generation to effect it. At any rate is it not a purely theoretical policy that which consists in proposing "to abandon Europe to its sorry fate," and in "turning one self towards colonial markets." An entirely new equipment would be required to carry it out, not only as regards distribution, but also as regards manufacturing, as goods required in new countries are totally different from those of which old countries in an advanced state of industry are in need. Besides, is it at all likely that the buying power of the dominions will increase in sufficient measure to absorb in the near future the greater part of the British exports? Imports of Australia per capita amount to an imposing figure, no doubt; but how many Australians are there? Five millions and a half at most. And how many will there be ten years hence? And then, who will guarantee that India will agree to remain the magnificent outlet she has heretofore been for England? As for Europe, who will seriously suggest that we should no longer concern ourselves about it, when even to this day it absorbs 35 per cent

United Kingdom
of British exports. Neither should we forget that its prosperity reacts on that of far away producers whose good will is most anxiously sought. Such were the anxieties to which the powerful Federation of British Industries gave expression on the eve of the assembling of the Imperial conference of 1923.
Those who are interested in this question I would refer to a work entitled "Interimperial Trade, First Interim Report, June 15, 1923," published by the Federation of British Industries.
We must note the essential difference which exists between the imperial preference enacted by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1897, and the policy of economic imperialism which the Conservative party wishes to sanction by the agreements submitted to us. Under the British preference of Laurier and his successors, England was granted advantages by Canada, in the form of customs privileges. While England, on the other hand, did not pledge herself to reciprocal obligations in theory; however, in practice England always granted us great advantages as to our exports. The short time allotted to me precludes my quoting statistics; however, all members of this house and all who are interested in economic questions are aware that we carried on a very profitable trade with England, long before these empire agreements were ever signed.
I shall borrow from a highly disinterested observer, a French economist, an appreciation of the British preference granted by Laurier.
Previous to quoting this article may I state that the Conservative party of today falls very short of the policy adopted by the same party in the past, and more particularly of the policy laid down by Cartier and Macdonald, those two great statesmen whose names appear in all the speeches of Conservatives. To remind hon. gentlemen how great is the difference between the policy of Cartier-Macdonald and the imperial policy of the present Conservative party, I shall refer to a letter published in the Canadian press in 1921, by the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve), in which he alludes to the military imperialism of his party. He stated, among other things, the following:
The Conservative party, in Quebec, for the last ten years, has estranged itself too much from the policy laid down by Cartier and Macdonald, and it has been more Tory than Conservative.
The following is what the French economist, to whom I referred a moment ago, stated:
It is known that for various reasons, in which loyalty plays an important part, but from which the hope of reciprocity is not excluded. Canada, in 1897, the Union of South Africa, in 1903, New Zealand, in 1907, Australia, in 1908, granted to British products
a tariff preference: the advantages in connection with this preference as applied to foreign imports is on an average of | in Canada and Australia, J to S in New Zealand, and i in South Africa. Certain crown colonies grant a greater preference, but India disassociates herself from this preference on English goods, and even is contemplating raising her tariff which would directly affect English products. The dominions showed the most good will. If in a general way they provided, by the establishment of an "intermediary tariff," for the possibility of negotiating trade conventions with foreign countries, they have, nevertheless, taken care, heretofore, that the imperial tariff -under reserve of isolated concessions-would exclusively apply to the mother country and the various parts of the empire. In agreement with them, the British government explains to outsiders, that the imperial preference is a domestic affair, and does not affect the clause of the most favoured nation.
It is known that the Imperial conference of 1930 was a failure. I shall not discuss the details of this conference, however, I shall refer those whom this question interests to the clear views of an economist who contributes to the editing of " lTllustration," in France, and to the monthly editions of Larousse, volume 8, December, 1930; these views were expressed after the Imperial conference and show that it was an actual failure.
We now come to the Imperial economic conference of 1932. The nations of the British Commonwealth gathered in Ottawa, forming a family pact, induced England to establish a tariff against the rest of the world. Following this conference the English people, who had already condemned the same policy, at the election of 1923, have not ceased to protest, and we witnessed the resignation of Liberal ministers forming part of the British National government and officially registering their protests.
It is unfortunate that Canada, by this economic imperialism, excludes the country which should ibe her best customer, the one with which, in the past, she carried on a profitable business, I refer to the United States.
Our trade with the United States follows so natural a course that the foreign policy of the United States has a great influence on Canadian affairs and is even felt in our elections. In fact, we can prove that the United States by their tariff policy of June, 1930,- a disastrous policy to Canada,-has greatly contributed to the advent to power of the Conservative party, in connection with the sale price of butter. We know that, in 1930, at a critical moment when the Canadian people were on the eve of going to the polls, the United States, by their tariff policy, prevented the entry of our dairy products into their country, while, in previous years, they

I am sure the house and the country must have been amused when the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) stated that he had prayed for the conference. I notice that he did not say that he had prayed for the success of the conference, and I imagine that his prayer must have been about as follows:
O Lord, come to us in this hour of humiliation, stay by us during this period of depression. Abide with us while we are in opposition.

Vouchsafe, O Lord, to ruin any attempt of the Conservative party to restore confidence in our land. Ruin, O Lord, the Conservative party and the Dominion of Canada if necessary to grant us a return to power. We ask this in the name of the King, Amen.
I had not intended and had little desire to take part in this debate, but I felt I should do so because of an article which appeared in the Border Cities Star of Tuesday, October 18. That issue contained a very fine picture of the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the article in question was headed, "No Tobacco Benefit." I might say to hon. members of the opposition that the Border Cities Star is far more complimentary to the leader of the opposition than the Vancouver Sun. As must have been observed by the right hon. leader of the opposition, the people of Essex county in western Ontario take very little stock in what he says. In 1930 the right hon. gentleman had the privilege of addressing an audience of 11,000 people in the town of Tilbury. When the right hon. gentleman became the leader of the government, Essex county polled a Liberal majority of 11,000, but in 1930, after being nine years in office, the same county gave a Conservative majority of 11,000. Consequently I think I am right in saying that the people in that county take with a grain of salt any version which the right hon. gentleman might give of things concerning their welfare. The article in question reads as follows:
No Tobacco Benefit
The agreement purports to be doing something for the tobacco growers for ten years. Notice how insidious the whole thing is. There is nothing in this clause that says it is necessary that any duty will be retained for ten years on tobacco. If the duty to other countries goes down, down goes the margin of preference. What benefit is that to the Canadian tobacco grower? Who is going to invest in large tobacco plants on the strength of that?
I say to the right hon. gentleman that that is absolutely not so. The preference given to the tobacco growers of Canada nnd the British Empire is not a specific rate per pound; it is based on an import duty against foreign tobacco entering the British isles. The previous tariff on raw leaf tobacco entering Great Britain was $1.96 per pound, but some years ago, in order to encourage the growing of a better grade of tobacco for the British market, the British colonies were given a preference of twenty-five per cent. At this time I shall not go into the tobacco question in detail, but if time permits before I conclude my remarks I will give further particulars as to the possibility of increasing our trade -with the British Empire.

I want to say to the hon. member for West Middlesex: If there -was an election today in western Ontario upon these proposals, no hon. member representing a rural constituency and opposing these agreements would be returned to parliament. The hon. gentleman went further:
Mr. Elliott spoke of the removal of the cattle embargo and claimed that its removal in 1923 was a greater achievement than the widening of the regulations attained at the imperial conference.
Why was it so great in 1923, and so unimportant in 1932? I cannot understand that. The hon. gentleman went on to say:

the government the hardship high tariffs were causing farmers.
Let me tell him of some of the hardships which high tariffs are causing the farmers of Essex county, and in which the farmers of his county are participating. I have under my hand a letter which came to me unsolicited, and which I shall read in a moment or so, to show what the conditions are in Essex county. The hon. gentleman went on:

Why, sir, there is not a member on the opposite side of the house who wants an election; not a solitary one; and there is no member on this side who wants an election. free entry of Canadian hams and bacon to the extent of 2,500,000 hundredweight be of interest to the farmers represented by the hon. member for West Middlesex. Would it be of interest to the farmers represented by the hon. member for West Lambton? I ask if the modification of regulations governing live cattle is of interest to western Ontario farmers. I ask the hon. members I have mentioned if the free entry of butter and cheese is in the interests of their constituents. I ask if the twentyTive per cent preference on Canadian tobacco in the British markets for ten years, brought about by legislation, is of interest to tobacco growing districts. I ask hon. members representing the tobacco sections of Ontario if this article in the agreement is in their interests?
Yesterday the hon. member for Norfolk-Elgin (Mr. Taylor) asked a silly question. I said at the time he asked it that representations such as he made had been made for ten years. For ten years application was made to the former government to bust the tobacco combine, and if the hon. member will stand with me I will do my part towards helping to bust any tobacco combine in the Dominion of Canada. I ask him, an hon. member from a tobacco constituency, if he appreciates the twenty-five per cent preference which is being made permanent by legislation. I know what he wants to say- it is this:	"Oh, we have had a twenty-five
per cent preference in the British market." I say to him certainly we have; I said that at the outset of my remarks, but I add that we never enjoyed that preference through legislation.

I want to ask the hon. member, if apples from Canada go into the British market free while from foreign countries there is a duty of 4s. 6d. per hundredweight, is that a benefit to the apple growers he represents? I ask all hon. members who represent farmers, for whom they say their hearts bleed, if there is any benefit to them in the preference on pears, plums, canned tomatoes, and ketchup. I am going to read an article in a moment pertaining to ketchup. Are they in favour of the free entry of eggs, against a duty on foreign eggs? I presume they are all going to vote against this agreement; consequently they are all opposed to a preference of 7 shillings a hundredweight on Canadian honey, and ten per cent on barley; they are opposed to the free entry of Canadian wheat against a general tariff of 3 pence per bushel. They are opposed to the free entry of wheat flour, rye, oats, shorts, and millings, oatmeal, peas, clover seed, hay, bran, rolled oats, et cetera. The}' are opposed to the free entry of unsweetened condensed milk. Yes, they are opposed to that, although there is a ten per cent general tariff. I presume, Mr. Speaker, they are opposed, as they have been for the last ten years, to anything that would be in the interests of the farmers they represent. The former government in its nine years in office did practically nothing but rest on its oars and let the market of western Ontario be swamped with surplus farm products from the United States.
[Mr. Gott.l
I want to read something which will indicate the benefit that the trade pact with Great Britain has already had on one huge industry in the riding which I have the honour to represent. I quote from the Border Cities Star of October 21, 1932, headed:
Gets Trade from U.S.
Leamington Plant to Handle All Heinz Export Trade Will be Increase
Overseas Orders Formerly Filled at Pittsburgh to Be Taken Over
Leamington, Oet. 21.-As a result of the action of the Ottawa conference, all ketchup produced by H. J. Heinz Company for export to the United Kingdom and European countries hereafter will be made at that concern's Leamington, Ont. plant.
Ketchup for export has been produced at Leamington in large quantities, but under orders just issued by the company there will be an important increase in production.
Export business formerly handled at Heinz plants in the United States will be transferred to the Leamington establishment, and, added to the present volume, will absorb the capacity production of that plant, which was built large enough to care for this increased demand upon it.
Heinz plant at Leamington is the largest producer of ketchup in the world, and has facilities to handle a million bushels of tomatoes a season. Anticipating present conditions, the company erected large additions and increased production facilities within the past two years.
The major part of the plant's ketchup production is consumed in England, but the consumption per capita of Heinz ketchup in Canada is the largest of any country in the world.
Within the past year, export demand for products of the Leamington plant has been of sufficient size to justify shipments of full cargoes directly by water from that point to England, while there has been a large increase in Canadian consumption.
Let me say, sir, that this government have launched a plan whereby they are expending a quarter of a million dollars in the town of Leamington for the purpose of erecting docks, at which large ocean going boats can load and unload, and those in charge of export expect to ship direct from the Heinz factory to Great Britain.
Another article that I desire to quote is headed:
Canadian Lumber Trade to Benefit by British Move
But Effects of Abrogation of Soviet Trade Treaty Will Not Be Seen For Some Months

That, however, was dealt with tonight by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White), who delivered, I believe, one of the sincerest speeches that has been delivered on these proposals. Many of the speeches made by hon. members opposite have been merely a waste of time. Some speakers have merely spoken to their constituents, some have spoken because the party whips put them on, whereas the party whips on this side requested us not to speak and I am speaking tonight against the advice of our whip.
I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that forty minutes is very little time within which to discuss an important resolution such as this. I said that if I had time I would discuss some details of the tobacco exports, and the possibilities before our tobacco industry in getting into the British market. As my time has almost expired I will only say that the imports of tobacco into Great Britain from the Dominion of Canada for the year 1932 have so far surpassed those of any other year. The Canadian tobacco grower is encouraged to such an extent that he believes there is a market in the United Kingdom and the empire for millions and millions of pounds of Canadian tobacco, because the British market consumes annually
230,000,000 pounds of which 200,000,000 pounds have heretofore been imported from the United States. With this twenty-five per cent preference made permanent for ten years the Canadian tobacco growers anticipate that they will enlarge their market and that within a few years the exports of raw leaf tobacco from Canada to' the Unitdd Kingdom, instead of being eight, nine or ten million pounds, will be at least 100,000,000 pounds a year.
